title: “WE MUST OBEY GOD RATHER THAN MEN” — BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE PEOPLE DEMANDING YOUR OBEDIENCE CLAIM TO SPEAK FOR GOD?
paragraphs: “WE MUST OBEY GOD RATHER THAN MEN” — BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE PEOPLE DEMANDING YOUR OBEDIENCE CLAIM TO SPEAK FOR GOD?
When submission becomes surrender to sin, when resistance becomes an act of faith, and when following Jesus costs you the approval of the very people you were taught to honor.
There is a kind of betrayal that hurts differently.
It happens when the person asking you to compromise your conscience is someone you were taught to respect.
A father whose approval you have spent your whole life trying to earn.
A pastor whose sermons once helped you survive your darkest season.
A husband who quotes Scripture while demanding something Scripture never gave him the right to demand.
A leader who speaks about loyalty but becomes angry whenever someone asks for accountability.
Or a government that expects Christians to remain silent when obedience to its commands would require disobedience to God.
And suddenly, you find yourself standing in a place you never imagined.
If you obey them, something inside you knows you will be betraying what God has revealed.
But if you refuse, you may lose relationships, reputation, opportunities, security, or even the community you once called home.
You pray.
You cry.
You search the Scriptures, hoping there might be a way to honor everyone without disappointing anyone.
Then five words confront you with a truth you can no longer avoid.
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29, KJV
But here is the question that can change everything.
What happens when the person you must respectfully refuse is someone God has commanded you to honor?
And how do you know whether your resistance is genuine obedience to Christ—or simply rebellion dressed in religious language?
Because not every act of submission is righteous.
And not every act of resistance is holy.
The difference may reveal whether Jesus truly has the highest authority in your life.
Imagine Jerusalem.
The city is restless. Religious authorities are increasingly alarmed by the growing proclamation that Jesus of Nazareth—the One crucified publicly—has risen from the dead.
The apostles have been preaching Christ.
People are hearing the Gospel. Lives are being changed. The name of Jesus is spreading.
And the religious authorities want it stopped.
The apostles are arrested and placed in public custody.
But during the night, an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors and commands them to return to the temple and proclaim the words of life.
Think about that.
They have already been imprisoned for preaching.
They know the danger.
They know the authorities are watching.
And the very next morning, they are standing in the temple, teaching again.
Not because they enjoy confrontation.
Not because they despise authority.
But because the risen Jesus has given them a commission no earthly authority can cancel.
When the apostles are brought before the council, the high priest confronts them.
“Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name?” — Acts 5:28, KJV
Notice the conflict.
The council had commanded silence.
Jesus had commanded witness.
Both commands could not be obeyed.
Peter and the apostles answered:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29, KJV
The original Greek reads:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei Theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
A careful translation is:
“It is necessary to obey God rather than human beings.”
The Greek word δεῖ (dei) communicates necessity or obligation. The verb πειθαρχεῖν (peitharchein) means to obey an authority.
Peter is not merely expressing a preference.
He is recognizing a binding obligation.
When a human command directly conflicts with God's command, obedience to God must take precedence.
But notice something equally important.
Peter does not say, “We obey God, therefore we never obey human authorities.”
He says, “We must obey God rather than human beings.”
That distinction matters enormously.
The apostles were not declaring that every personal disagreement justified defiance. They were responding to a direct prohibition against fulfilling Christ's commission.
And if we miss that context, we can turn a courageous declaration of faith into an excuse for pride, disorder, or spiritual recklessness.
Because the same Bible that records Peter's resistance also commands Christians to honor legitimate authority.
Romans 13:1 teaches:
“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.”
First Peter 2:17 says:
“Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.”
These verses were not written to Christians living under perfectly righteous governments.
They were written in a world where Roman power could be harsh, unjust, and hostile to believers.
Submission was not merely a principle for convenient circumstances.
It was part of Christian witness.
And yet the apostles resisted when authorities demanded that they stop proclaiming Jesus.
Is Scripture contradicting itself?
No.
Scripture is teaching something deeper than unquestioning compliance or automatic rebellion.
Human authority is real, but it is never ultimate.
God is the source of all rightful authority.
And no person who exercises authority receives permission from God to command what God forbids or forbid what God commands.
That includes presidents.
Pastors.
Parents.
Husbands.
Employers.
And every other person entrusted with responsibility over someone else's life.
Authority is not ownership.
Leadership is not lordship.
And submission is not the surrender of your conscience to another human being.
Only Jesus Christ is Lord.
But before you use that truth against someone else, allow it to examine your own heart.
Because sometimes we resist authority not because God has commanded us to, but because we hate being corrected.
Sometimes we call accountability persecution.
Sometimes we call our preferences convictions.
Sometimes we confuse discomfort with oppression.
And sometimes the words “God told me” become a shield against anyone who dares to question our decisions.
That is not the courage of Acts 5.
That is the danger of making ourselves the final authority while claiming to defend God's authority.
The Christian who says, “I must obey God rather than men,” must first be willing to ask:
Am I actually obeying what God has revealed in Scripture?
Or am I using God's name to justify what I already wanted to do?
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
Because genuine biblical resistance begins with submission—not submission to human control, but submission to the Word of God.
And there is an ancient story that exposes just how costly that submission can become.
Long before Peter stood before the council, three young Jewish men stood before a king whose command was unmistakable.
Bow before the golden image.
Or burn.
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were living in Babylon, far from their homeland.
They were not refusing every responsibility within the empire. They had served in positions of administration.
But when King Nebuchadnezzar demanded worship that belonged to God alone, the boundary became clear.
Their answer was astonishing.
“Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace...” — Daniel 3:17, KJV
Then came the words that reveal the difference between faith and bargaining.
“But if not...” — Daniel 3:18, KJV
But if not.
If God does not rescue us.
If the flames are real.
If obedience costs us everything.
We still will not worship your image.
They did not make faithfulness dependent on a miracle.
They did not say God owed them survival.
They trusted God's power without presuming to control God's decision.
And that is where many modern ideas about spiritual victory collapse.
We sometimes imagine that if we obey God, every door must open, every enemy must retreat, every relationship must be restored, and every sacrifice must produce visible success.
But biblical faithfulness is not a contract guaranteeing earthly comfort.
Sometimes obedience leads to deliverance.
Sometimes obedience leads to suffering.
The three men were delivered from the furnace.
Stephen was killed while bearing witness to Christ.
Peter was miraculously released from prison in Acts 12.
James, the brother of John, was executed earlier in that same chapter.
The Bible refuses to let us measure God's faithfulness by the absence of pain.
And that brings us to a truth some Christians desperately need to hear.
You can be in the will of God and still be deeply misunderstood.
You can tell the truth respectfully and still be rejected.
You can refuse to participate in wrongdoing and still lose your position.
You can establish a necessary boundary and still be accused of dishonor.
You can follow Jesus faithfully and still grieve what obedience has cost you.
But pain alone does not prove that your resistance was righteous.
And opposition alone does not prove that you were wrong.
The question is whether your actions are faithful to Christ.
Consider the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1.
Pharaoh commanded that Hebrew baby boys be killed.
Shiphrah and Puah feared God and did not carry out that murderous command.
The Hebrew text of Exodus 1:17 says:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
Vattirena hamyalledot et-ha'Elohim.
“The midwives feared God.”
That phrase matters.
Their refusal was rooted in reverence for God, not merely contempt for Pharaoh.
They recognized a moral obligation greater than the king's command.
Their actions protected vulnerable lives.
And Scripture explicitly commends their fear of God.

But we must read carefully. Exodus also records the midwives' response to Pharaoh when questioned. The text commends their fear of God and their refusal to carry out the killing; it does not require us to conclude that every detail of their explanation was an approved model for deception.
Faithful interpretation does not need to exaggerate a passage to make it powerful.
The truth is already powerful enough.
A ruler commanded murder.
Two women feared God.
Children lived.
And heaven did not mistake their refusal for sinful rebellion.
Now bring that truth into the places where people actually struggle.
What if a supervisor orders you to falsify records?
What if a church leader pressures you to conceal abuse to protect the ministry's reputation?
What if a family member demands that you participate in fraud because “family comes first”?
What if someone uses Scripture to demand silence about exploitation?
What if the person exercising authority tells you that asking for help is the same as dishonoring God?
This is where theology stops being an argument on a page.
This is where someone may be sitting alone at night, trembling over a decision.
Because the consequences are real.
And they need more than a dramatic slogan.
They need biblical truth applied with wisdom.
If a command requires you to sin, you must not obey that command.
But that does not mean every disagreement with authority creates a duty to resist.
A leader making an inconvenient decision is not necessarily committing injustice.
A parent setting a reasonable boundary is not necessarily exercising spiritual control.
A church correcting genuine wrongdoing is not necessarily persecuting someone.
And a government enforcing an ordinary law is not automatically opposing God because the law is unpopular.
The Christian must distinguish between commands that are sinful, commands that are legitimate, and matters where wisdom, conscience, and lawful processes require careful discernment.
That distinction protects us from two dangerous extremes.
Blind obedience that enables evil.
And reckless resistance that baptizes self-will as righteousness.
Both can dishonor Christ.
And both can wound people.
Jesus Himself shows us a better way.
He submitted to the Father's will completely.
He honored the law of God.
He taught His followers to render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God (Mark 12:17).
He paid the temple tax in Matthew 17:24–27, even while explaining the freedom of the sons.
He also confronted religious hypocrisy.
He exposed leaders who placed crushing burdens on others.
He refused to let human traditions nullify God's commandments.
In Mark 7:8, Jesus said:
“For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men...”
Here is the tragedy.
People can become so committed to defending a religious system that they begin resisting the very Word of God they claim to protect.
A tradition can become more important than truth.
A leader's reputation can become more important than wounded people.
An institution's survival can become more important than repentance.
And suddenly, the name of God is being used to defend something God Himself condemns.
That should terrify every person entrusted with spiritual leadership.
Because Jesus did not come to create a religious hierarchy in which the powerful are untouchable.
He said:
“Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.” — Matthew 20:27, KJV
And in Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted the domineering leadership of worldly rulers with the servant-hearted leadership expected among His disciples.
Christian leadership is not a license to dominate.
It is a call to serve.
A pastor is accountable to the Chief Shepherd.
A husband is accountable to Christ.
A parent is accountable to God for how children are treated.
A public official remains accountable to the moral authority of God.
And every Christian remains responsible for personal obedience to the Lord.
Consider the word translated “submit” in passages such as Ephesians 5:21.
The Greek reads:
Ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ.
Hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”
The verb ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō) concerns placing oneself in an ordered relationship or being subject to another.
Its precise application depends on context.
It does not mean that every authority relationship is identical, nor does it erase the distinct instructions that follow in Ephesians 5 and 6.
But neither does it grant unlimited power to the person receiving submission.
In the very same passage, husbands are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
That is sacrificial love.
Not intimidation.
Not cruelty.
Not manipulation.
Not the exploitation of vulnerability.
And parents are instructed not to provoke their children to wrath but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4).
Biblical authority carries obligations.
It does not exist for the personal gratification of the powerful.
If you have been taught that submission means accepting abuse, participating in sin, or surrendering your ability to seek protection, you have been given a distorted picture of biblical submission.
Seeking safety, reporting a crime, or refusing a sinful demand is not automatically rebellion against God.

When someone is in danger, immediate safety matters. Qualified pastoral care, appropriate civil authorities, and professional support can be important. Scripture must never be used to pressure a person to remain in immediate danger or conceal serious wrongdoing.
And yet there is another side to this truth.
Resistance can become sinful when it is driven by vengeance.
When it relies on lies.
When it humiliates people for pleasure.
When it treats every authority figure as an enemy.
When it refuses correction.
Or when it seeks power rather than righteousness.
Remember what Peter and the apostles did after declaring that they must obey God rather than men.
They did not respond by calling for personal revenge.
They proclaimed Jesus.
They testified that God had raised the One whom the authorities had crucified.
They announced repentance and forgiveness.
Acts 5:31 says that God exalted Jesus:
“...to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.”
Do not miss this.
At the center of their confrontation was not their personal freedom.
It was the crucified and risen Christ.
Even while confronting the leaders responsible for opposing Jesus, the apostles proclaimed a Savior who gives repentance and forgiveness.
What astonishing grace.
The people hearing Peter's words were not beyond the reach of the Gospel.
The same Jesus they had rejected was being proclaimed as the One through whom forgiveness could be received.
That is the heart of Christian resistance.
Not merely standing against what is wrong.
But bearing witness to the One who makes sinners right with God.
Not merely exposing darkness.
But pointing people toward the Light.
Not merely winning an argument.
But remaining faithful to Jesus.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe you are not the person being pressured to compromise.
Maybe you are the person who has been pressuring others.
Maybe someone tried to tell you the truth, and you called them disrespectful.
Maybe someone asked you to be accountable, and you called it disloyalty.
Maybe you used your position, your knowledge of Scripture, or your influence to silence a person who was already hurting.
Maybe you were more concerned about being obeyed than about being Christlike.
If that is you, there is still a way forward.
But it begins with repentance.
Not excuses.
Not another sermon about submission.
Not a demand that the wounded person forgive immediately and act as though nothing happened.
Repentance means acknowledging sin, turning from it, accepting accountability, and pursuing whatever restitution and change are appropriate.
Forgiveness is central to the Gospel, but forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence, automatically restore trust, or require someone to return to an unsafe situation.
Grace is not permission to continue harming people.
Grace calls us out of sin.
And perhaps you are on the other side.
You have spent years trying to be good.
Trying to be respectful.
Trying to be the Christian who never causes problems.
You have swallowed words that should have been spoken.
You have apologized for things that were not your fault.
You have mistaken the absence of conflict for the presence of peace.
And now, for the first time, you are asking whether obedience to Jesus might require you to say no.
If Scripture has made the matter clear, you do not need to turn your refusal into hatred.
You can honor someone without agreeing with everything they demand.
You can speak truth without cruelty.
You can seek counsel without surrendering your conscience.
You can refuse wrongdoing while praying for the person who pressured you.
You can accept that someone may be disappointed in you without concluding that God is disappointed in you.
But remain humble.
Test your motives.
Listen to wise correction.
Examine the full counsel of Scripture rather than one verse isolated from its context.
Where circumstances are complicated, seek trustworthy, biblically grounded counsel that does not have a conflict of interest.
And remember that the duty to obey God never gives us permission to become careless with the truth.
The apostle Peter later wrote:
“But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer...” — 1 Peter 3:15, KJV
He continued by emphasizing meekness, reverence, and a good conscience.
The man who declared that God must be obeyed above human beings also taught Christians to defend their hope with humility.
Conviction without arrogance.
Courage without cruelty.
Faithfulness without vengeance.
That is not weakness.
That is spiritual maturity.
And it leads us to the most important scene in this entire conversation.
A garden.
A night of anguish.
A Savior praying as the cross draws near.
Jesus knows the suffering ahead.
He knows the betrayal.
He knows the false accusations.
He knows the cruelty of sinful human authorities.
And in Gethsemane, He prays:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
Here is the obedience that saves us.
Not our courage.
Not our resistance.
Not our ability to recognize every moral conflict correctly.
But the perfect obedience of Jesus Christ.
He did not sin.
He did not compromise the Father's will.
He did not abandon His mission when obedience became costly.
And when the authorities came to arrest Him, He did not need to prove His power through violent retaliation.
He willingly walked toward the cross in fulfillment of the Father's saving purpose.
Philippians 2:8 says:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
The Greek expression is:
γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου
genomenos hypēkoos mechri thanatou.
“Becoming obedient unto death.”
This is the obedience at the center of our redemption.
Jesus was not merely teaching us how to resist unjust authority.
He was accomplishing what no sinner could accomplish.
He obeyed the Father perfectly.
He bore our sins.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not that brave people earn salvation by resisting evil.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ saves sinners by grace through faith, and those who belong to Him are called to walk in obedience.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase God's acceptance.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by His grace.
That distinction changes everything.
Because even the strongest Christian has failed.
Perhaps you remained silent when you should have spoken.
Perhaps you resisted when you should have listened.
Perhaps fear controlled you.
Perhaps pride controlled you.
Perhaps you betrayed your conscience to preserve a relationship.
Perhaps you wounded someone while claiming to defend the truth.
There is mercy for repentant sinners.
Remember Peter.
The same Peter who boldly declared, “We ought to obey God rather than men,” once denied knowing Jesus three times.
He knew what it meant to collapse under pressure.
He knew the shame of choosing personal safety over public loyalty to Christ.
And yet the risen Jesus restored him.
John 21 records Jesus questioning Peter's love and commissioning him to care for His sheep.
The man who once denied Jesus would become a witness who refused to stop proclaiming His name.
That is not a story about a naturally fearless man.
That is a story about the grace of a faithful Savior.
The same Jesus who forgave Peter's denial strengthened Peter's witness.
And He is still able to transform people who have failed Him.
Maybe you need courage today.
Maybe you need humility.
Maybe you need to repent for misusing authority.
Maybe you need to stop confusing obedience to a person with obedience to God.
Maybe you need to stop calling your own stubbornness spiritual warfare.
Or maybe you need to hear something that fear has kept you from believing.
Your loyalty to Jesus is not measured by how successfully you please every person around you.
It is measured by faithfulness to the Lord who bought you with His blood.
And faithfulness sometimes means submitting when your pride wants to rebel.
Sometimes it means speaking when fear wants you to remain silent.
Sometimes it means accepting correction.
Sometimes it means refusing a sinful command.
Sometimes it means seeking protection.
Sometimes it means enduring consequences without surrendering your convictions.
And sometimes it means admitting that you were wrong.
All of it must be brought beneath the lordship of Christ.
Not the lordship of personal feelings.
Not the lordship of public opinion.
Not the lordship of religious personalities.
Christ alone.
So before you declare, “I will obey God rather than men,” ask yourself something that may be even more revealing.
Am I willing to obey God when His Word corrects me, too?
Because it is easy to celebrate Peter when we imagine ourselves standing beside him.
It is harder to recognize that sometimes we are the ones trying to silence a truth we do not want to hear.
Sometimes we are the frightened disciple.
Sometimes we are the controlling authority.
Sometimes we are the person resisting correction.
Sometimes we are the wounded believer who needs courage.
And every one of us needs the same Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The One who confronts our sin without abandoning His mercy.
The One who calls us to repentance without closing the door of grace.
The One who does not merely expose what is broken, but redeems those who turn to Him.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to turn Scripture into outrage for attention.
Not to teach people to hate authority.
But to keep bringing hearts back to Jesus Christ, the authority of His Word, the seriousness of sin, the necessity of repentance, and the breathtaking hope of the Gospel.
And if this article has reached a place in your life that you rarely talk about, please do not rush past it.
Be honest before God.
Have you been submitting to something He never commanded?
Have you been resisting something He clearly requires?
Have you been afraid to stand for the truth?
Or have you been using the language of faith to protect your own pride?
And if God has brought you through a season where faithfulness was costly, consider sharing a testimony that could strengthen someone who is still walking through theirs.
There may be someone reading the comments who needs to know they are not alone.
Someone who has been told that asking questions is rebellion.
Someone who has confused fear with reverence.
Someone who needs to discover that Christ calls His people to truth and love together.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them—not to embarrass them or expose their struggle, but to encourage them toward the Word of God.
A single share may place Scripture before someone who would never think to search for it.
It may reach a discouraged believer, a questioning young person, a struggling family, or someone who has almost given up on church because of what happened to them.
We cannot know what God will do through one act of sharing.
But we can faithfully make the truth available.
Because the real test of conviction often comes long after the emotion of reading has faded.
There is also a deeper invitation for those who want to grow with us and help sustain this work.
Gospel Warrior is seeking to build a community where believers are strengthened through serious discipleship, not merely momentary inspiration.
It is a practical way to help sustain and expand Gospel-centered teaching, develop more discipleship resources, and make biblical encouragement available to more people.
God loves a cheerful giver, not one who gives under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And the Gospel must never be presented as something that can be purchased.
Salvation is freely given through Jesus Christ.
The free resources remain a genuine part of our mission.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, or thoughtful gifts that point people back to Christ.
You are not less faithful.
You are not less welcome.
And your place in the family of God is not measured by your financial ability.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
The goal is not to make people dependent on Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people to Jesus, teach them to examine the Scriptures, and encourage them to grow in a faithful local church and in genuine Christian community.
Because a ministry has succeeded spiritually not when people become dependent on its platform, but when people are growing in their knowledge, love, and obedience to Christ.
And now, return to that room in Jerusalem.
The apostles are standing before powerful men.
Their future is uncertain.
They know what the authorities have commanded.
They know what Jesus has commanded.
They must decide whom they will obey.
The council eventually has them beaten and orders them again not to speak in the name of Jesus.
Acts 5:41 records that the apostles departed, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name.
And verse 42 tells us that they continued daily, in the temple and from house to house, teaching and preaching Jesus Christ.
They did not stop.
But do you see what made their courage extraordinary?
It was not the absence of fear.
It was not hatred of the authorities.
It was not the desire to become famous for resistance.
It was their allegiance to the risen Lord.
They knew the One who had conquered death.
And because of Him, they could face the consequences of obedience.
That same Lord calls us today.
Not every Christian will stand before a council.
Not every believer will face imprisonment.
But every disciple will eventually confront the question of ultimate allegiance.
Whose approval do I fear losing most?
Whose voice has the final word over my conscience?
Whose commands govern my choices?
And when God's Word confronts what I want, will I still call Him Lord?
The answer is not found in how loudly we declare our convictions.
It is found in whether we are willing to follow Jesus with humility, truth, courage, repentance, and love.
So when the world demands compromise, remember Peter.
When obedience becomes costly, remember the three men before the furnace.
When the powerful demand wrongdoing, remember the Hebrew midwives.
When pride makes resistance attractive, remember the command to honor rightful authority.
When fear makes silence tempting, remember the apostles.
When you fail, remember Peter's restoration.
And above all, remember Jesus.
The obedient Son.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One whose authority is greater than every earthly throne.
The One whose grace is greater than the shame of repentant sinners.
The One who calls you not merely to resist what is evil, but to belong entirely to Him.
Because the greatest question is not whether you have the courage to stand against men.
It is whether your heart has truly bowed before Christ.
You may lose the approval of people by obeying Jesus—but never let the fear of losing people make you forget the Savior who gave Himself to redeem you.
